client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. The sadness just kind of sits on my chest, and I can't shake it, but honestly what's eating at me even more is watching my mom fall apart and not knowing what to do or say to help her. I'm not even sure talking about it here is going to change anything, but I didn't know where else to turn.
therapist: I'm really glad you reached out, even through the doubt that it might help — that took courage, and the weight you're carrying right now, grieving your grandmother while also watching your mom struggle, sounds genuinely exhausting and lonely. It makes so much sense that the sadness feels stuck, like it has nowhere to go when you're also trying to be strong for someone else. Can you tell me a little more about what goes through your mind in those moments when you're with your mom and feel unsure of what to do — what does that inner voice tend to say to you?

client: When I'm with my mom and she starts crying or just goes really quiet, there's this voice in my head that says I should have the right words, like I'm failing her if I just sit there not knowing what to say. And then I start second-guessing everything — if I bring up grandma, is that going to make it worse, but if I don't, am I just pretending nothing happened? It ends up feeling like whatever I do is the wrong choice, and I leave feeling guilty and kind of hollow.
therapist: That "whatever I do is wrong" feeling is such a painful trap to be caught in, and it makes sense you leave those moments feeling hollow — you're essentially holding yourself to an impossible standard where silence fails her and speaking might hurt her. I'd gently want to explore that belief that you *should* have the right words — where do you think that expectation comes from, and is there a part of you that can imagine that simply being present, even quietly, might actually be offering your mom something real? What do you think she might say if you asked her what she actually needs from you right now?

client: I think the expectation probably comes from being the "responsible one" in the family — I've always been the person who figures things out and holds it together, so falling short of that feels like a big deal. But honestly, the idea of just being present without saying anything useful feels almost too simple, like I'd be doing nothing. And asking her directly what she needs... I don't know, that scares me a little, because what if she says something I can't give her?
therapist: There's something really meaningful in what you just named — that "doing nothing" feels like failing, when in reality, staying present with someone in pain is one of the hardest and most loving things a person can do, and it's far from nothing. And that fear of asking your mom what she needs makes a lot of sense — underneath it sounds like a worry that you might discover a limit to what you can offer, which would feel like another kind of failure for someone who's always been the one to hold things together. I'm curious, though — can you think of a time when *you* were struggling and what you needed most from someone wasn't a solution, but something simpler?

client: Actually, yeah — when I was going through a really rough patch a few years ago, I remember just wanting someone to sit with me and not try to fix it or tell me it would be okay. So I hear what you're saying, and intellectually it makes sense. But it still feels different when it's my mom, because she's the parent, and some part of me feels like the roles are supposed to be reversed — I'm not sure I know how to just be her kid and grieve alongside her instead of trying to manage everything.
therapist: You just made a really powerful connection — you *know* what presence feels like from the inside, which means you already understand what your mom might need more than you're giving yourself credit for. That shift you're describing, from being the child to feeling like you have to be the caretaker, is such a common and quietly painful thing that happens in grief, like the ground beneath the relationship has shifted and nobody told you the new rules. I wonder — what might it feel like, even just for a moment, to let yourself be her child again and grieve *with* her rather than *for* her?

client: Honestly, just imagining that makes my eyes sting a little, which I wasn't expecting. I think it might feel like a relief, but also really scary — like if I let myself be the grieving kid instead of the one holding it together, something might fall apart that I won't be able to put back together. I guess I'm not sure I trust myself to fall apart even a little without it becoming too much.
therapist: That sting in your eyes is telling you something true — there's real grief in there that hasn't had permission to surface yet, and the fact that imagining relief also feels terrifying makes complete sense for someone who's spent so long being the one who holds things together. That fear that falling apart "a little" might become "too much" is worth gently examining though — because in my experience, the feelings we keep tightly managed tend to grow heavier over time, while the ones we allow even a small amount of space often don't swallow us the way we fear they will. What do you think has taught you that your own grief is something that needs to be contained — has it ever actually "become too much" before, or is that more of a fear that's never really been tested?

client: When I actually think about it, I'm not sure it has ever truly become too much — I've always managed to pull myself back before finding out. But that almost makes it worse, because I've never actually tested the limit, so I've just been assuming the worst without any real evidence. I think somewhere along the way I just decided that being the strong one was safer than finding out what happens if I'm not, and now I don't even know who I am without that role.
therapist: What you just said is genuinely significant — you've identified, with real clarity, that the belief keeping you locked in this role has never actually been tested, which in CBT terms means it's been running your life as if it were fact when it's really just an old, protective assumption. And that last part, not knowing who you are without the "strong one" role, that's not a small thing to sit with, but it's also an incredibly honest and important place to have arrived at. I'm wondering — if being the strong one is a role you took on rather than who you fundamentally are, what small, safe moment this week might give you just a tiny bit of space to exist outside of it?

client: I want to say yes to that, but I'm already trying to think of what that would even look like and coming up blank, which maybe says something in itself. Part of me worries that any moment I try to "step out of the role" I'll just end up performing being vulnerable rather than actually feeling it, because being in control is so automatic for me now. I guess I'm not sure how you practice something like that without it feeling forced or like just another task I have to get right.
therapist: That worry about "performing" vulnerability rather than genuinely feeling it is such an insightful thing to notice, and honestly, the fact that you're already anticipating that trap shows just how deep the pattern of control runs — but it also means you're watching yourself with real honesty, which is different from just being on autopilot. Here's a gentle reframe though: what if practicing this doesn't have to look like a brave, visible moment of "being vulnerable," but could start as something quieter and internal, like simply noticing when you feel something and not immediately moving to manage it — just letting it be there for a few seconds without fixing it. What do you think it would feel like to set the bar that small, not as another task to get right, but just as a tiny experiment in curiosity about yourself?

client: Setting the bar that small does make it feel slightly less terrifying, I'll admit that. But I'm already noticing my brain wanting to turn "just observe the feeling for a few seconds" into a checklist item I need to execute correctly, which is kind of funny and also a little frustrating. I think I can try it, but I'm genuinely not sure I'll be able to tell the difference between actually feeling something and just watching myself feel something from a safe distance.
therapist: There's something genuinely warm and hopeful in the fact that you can laugh a little at your brain trying to turn "stop managing" into something to manage — that self-awareness is actually a sign of real contact with yourself, not distance from it. And that question of whether you're "actually feeling" versus "watching yourself feel" is one that even experienced meditators and therapists wrestle with, so you're in good company — but I'd also gently suggest that noticing you're watching from a distance *is itself* a feeling, a kind of emotional data, not a failure of the exercise. What if the goal this week isn't to feel the "right" way, but just to get curious about whatever shows up, even if what shows up is the familiar urge to observe from behind the glass?

client: Framing it as curiosity rather than getting it right does actually land differently for me — it takes some of the pressure off in a way I wasn't expecting. I think I can sit with that, even if part of me is still a little skeptical that noticing "I'm watching from behind the glass" counts as real progress. But I guess that skepticism is probably just another thing to get curious about rather than something I need to resolve before I'm allowed to start.
therapist: What you just said at the end there is actually quite beautiful — you caught the skepticism, named it, and then turned the same curiosity lens onto it without needing to defeat it first, which is exactly the shift we've been talking about, and you did it naturally, mid-sentence. That's not a small thing, even if it doesn't feel dramatic. As you move through this week, I'm wondering — when that skeptical voice shows up and says "this doesn't count as real progress," what might it feel like to respond to it the way you'd respond to your mom in her grief, with presence rather than the pressure to fix it?

client: That parallel actually stopped me for a second, because I hadn't connected those two things at all — the way I treat my own doubt and the way I'm trying to show up for my mom. It's a little uncomfortable to realize I might be more patient and gentle with her grief than I've ever been with anything going on inside myself. I think I can try to hold that this week, though I suspect the skeptical voice is going to be a lot louder and more convincing in the moment than it is right now sitting here talking about it.
therapist: That moment of recognition — that you've been extending a grace to your mom that you've rarely turned inward — is one of the most significant things you've uncovered today, and it makes sense it feels a little uncomfortable, because it's true and it matters. You're right that the skeptical voice will likely feel louder and more convincing when you're alone with it, but you've already shown today that you can notice it, name it, and not be completely ruled by it — and that's a real skill you're building, not just a good conversation. As you go into the week, I want to leave you with one small anchor: when that voice gets loud, see if you can ask yourself, "would I say this to my mom right now?" — and notice what that question does.
